content.content:
./.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml
# Build the Linux home-manager closures and push them to attic, so
# `home-manager switch` on the boxes downloads instead of compiling.
#
# mari (aarch64-darwin) is omitted — an x86_64-linux job can't build darwin.
# Cluster-side details and the traps behind the settings here:
# docs/forgejo-dotfiles-ci.md in the kube repo.
name: nix-home

on:
  push:
    branches: [master]
    paths:
      - "flake.nix"
      - "flake.lock"
      - "*.nix"
      - "home/**"
      - "patches/**"
      - ".forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml"
  # Forgejo has no re-run API; dispatch is the only way to retry.
  workflow_dispatch:

# A closure build is long, and two at once share one dind cgroup — so the group
# stays, and it still serializes. But it queues rather than cancels: cancelling
# discarded runs 58, 59 and 60 mid-build, and `hms` now blocks on the run for its
# own commit, which a follow-up push would otherwise kill under it. Queued runs
# still supersede each other, so this cannot pile up.
concurrency:
  group: nix-home-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

content.text:
**CI went red on a network blip, not on the diff. Retry dispatched and running.**

1. **Root cause:** `bun-linux-x64-1.4.2.tgz` — four consecutive `curl: (7) Failed to connect to registry.npmjs.org:443`. Everything downstream (bun-compiler → hunkdiff 0.23.0 → home-manager-generation) failed with "1 dependency failed."
2. **Why it's transient, not my change:** 126 other npmjs tarball fetches in the same run succeeded, including `mcode-0.6.5-npm-deps` and `claude-agent-acp-0.88.0-npm-deps` — both of my bumps built fine. Only that one fetch lost its connection.
3. **Why it needed building at all:** the `hunk` input bump (a3321c8 → 9566e33) produced hunkdiff 0.23.0, which isn't in attic yet, so its bun toolchain had to be fetched fresh.
4. **Retry path:** the workflow has no re-run API — `.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml:19` says dispatch is the only way — so I dispatched `nix-home.yml` on master and `hms` is now waiting on that run.

Nothing was switched; the commits are pushed and `origin/master` is at `910b012e`.

Next: I'll report when the retry lands. If the same bun fetch fails again, that's a real runner egress problem rather than a blip, and I'll bring it to you instead of retrying a third time.

in
{
  imports = [ sops-nix.homeManagerModules.sops walker.homeManagerModules.default zen-browser.homeModules.default ./antigravity.nix ./opencode.nix ./pi.nix ./cursor-agent.nix ./kimi-code.nix ./even-terminal.nix ./mcode.nix ];

  home.stateVersion = "26.05";

=== 2218-2292 ===
  # `herdr integration install pi` (v7); self-contained (no config registration
  # needed) and inert unless HERDR_ENV=1. Regenerate and bump if `herdr
  # integration status` reports it outdated.
  home.file.".pi/agent/extensions/herdr-agent-state.ts".source =
    ./home/.pi/agent/extensions/herdr-agent-state.ts;

  # ── herdr integration (mcode) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  # Hand-rolled — herdr 0.9.1 has no built-in mcode integration, and `mcode`
  # (MiniMax Code, npm `@minimax-ai/code`) is the only MiniMax-shaped TUI in
  # this repo that ships an extension surface herdr does not already cover.
  #
  # Layout: mcode's `local` marketplace is `~/.minimax/plugins/`. Dropping a
  # directory with `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` plus a matching
  # `hooks/hooks.json` there auto-installs and enables it on the next
  # `mcode plugin list` — no `mcode plugin add` step. mcode reads the
  # generated plugin via its `CLAUDE_CODE` loader path (the `defaultPath`
  # for that source format) and emits the hook wanting Claude-Code-shaped
  # JSON on stdin, with `$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` substituted into the
  # `command` field. Verified by running `mcode exec` against this exact
  # payload — SessionStart / UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse / PostToolUse /
  # Stop / Notification all fire as expected. SessionEnd is registered as
  # a hook in `hooks.json` so when mcode grows one (today it does not),
  # `pane.release_agent` fires immediately and the agent slot in the
  # sidebar disappears without waiting for herdr's prompt-return safety
  # net. Until then, that safety net ("clear the agent once the pane is
  # back at its shell prompt") is what cleans the pane up — and it only
  # fires when herdr recognises the source, which is why the script uses

git add home.nix && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
drop mcode

Removes MiniMax Code entirely: the `mcode.nix` module (derivation, the
nodejs_22 pin, the better-sqlite3 GC stress check and the provider-registration
activation), its vendored npm lockfile, `mcode-gc-stress.cjs`, the hand-rolled
herdr integration under `home/.minimax/`, the import, and the package entry.

The MiniMax-M3 wiring in `opencode.nix` and `pi.nix` stays -- those point at
Modular's own deployments and have nothing to do with this CLI. The shared
`~/.config/local-auto-mode/api-key` stays too; opencode and pi still read it,
mcode was only ever a third consumer.

Nothing else in the repo referenced it: `grep -ri mcode` outside .git/result
now returns nothing.

Leftover runtime state in `~/.minimax/` is not touched by this -- the
activation step that materialised the plugin is gone, but what it already
wrote is live-home state, not something the repo should delete behind your
back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -1 && git status --porcelain

entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID ("name@team") or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/systematic-debugging

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**A fix you cannot explain is a guess wearing a diff.** Until the failure
happens on demand and you can say *mechanistically* why, any change you make is
as likely to hide the bug as to remove it. Follow the spirit, not the letter:
running the reproduction once, seeing red, and then fixing what you *assumed*
was wrong satisfies the ordering and proves nothing. The rule is that the cause
you fix is the cause you demonstrated.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** They will not have your hunch, your scrollback, or the shape you
recognized. They get the reproduction command, the cause you wrote down, and the
test you added — anything you only knew is lost at the phase boundary.

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIX BEFORE A REPRODUCTION AND A MECHANISTIC CAUSE.
```

No exceptions:

- **Do not act on a shape you recognize.** A failure matching one you have seen
  before is a reason to *suspect* a cause, not a reason to skip confirming it.
  Go read this instance's fixture, input, or state and confirm it is that bug.
  Recognition works on the assertion output; the bug lives somewhere you have
  not looked yet.
- **Do not read a conditional instruction as permission to skip its condition.**
  *"If it's the off-by-one, just fix it"* waives re-litigating the fix once the
  cause is confirmed — it never waives confirming it. Establish the antecedent
  yourself, then take the permission it grants.
- **Do not let a deadline shorten the verification.** After the fix, re-run the
  original trigger **and** the full suite — the scope
  `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick under time
  pressure. The clock does not change which tests can catch what this fix
  disturbed. If the full suite genuinely cannot be run here, name the exact
  command you did not run and do not report the bug as fixed.
- **Do not start fix #4.** Three *failed fixes* — the unit is defined in step 6 —
  means your model of the system is wrong, not that the fourth guess is due.
  Stop, say so, and question the design with whoever owns it before changing
  another line.
- **Do not substitute reasoning for a reproduction.** If you cannot trigger the
  failure on demand, that is the finding to report. Keep narrowing — smaller
  input, more logging, a read-only explorer — and stop before shipping a fix
  you cannot verify.

## Announce

Say this out loud when you start, before the first edit:

```
Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each bug you work, not once for the session. If you
fall back to `CHECKLIST.md` at a repo root, do not commit it.

1. **Reproduce.** Get a reliable, minimal trigger and record the exact command
   and its output. A bug you cannot reproduce on demand is a bug you cannot
   prove you fixed.
2. **Isolate.** Narrow to the smallest input, file, or code path that still
   shows it. Bisect, add logging, or dispatch a **read-only explorer** to map
   the suspect area. Fan-out investigation belongs to read-only explorers (e.g.
   `explore-mcp`), never to parallel writers — you keep the editing, which is
   what keeps drovr's single-writer rule intact.
3. **Root-cause.** Explain *why* it happens, mechanistically. "Adding this line
   makes it go away" is not a cause. Keep going until the explanation predicts
   the observed behavior exactly — including the parts you were not chasing.
4. **Fix.** Make the minimal change that addresses the cause, not the symptom.
5. **Verify.** Re-run your original trigger and confirm it is gone, then run the
   **full suite** — unconditionally, whatever the clock says.
   `drovr:verification-before-completion` owns what "full" means here and what
   evidence it takes; do not substitute a narrower scope you picked yourself.
   Add or fix a test that would have caught it.
6. **Escalate at three failed fixes.** A **failed fix** is one change you made,
   ran, and watched leave the failure in place. That is the unit — not edits, not
   builds, not ideas you considered and dropped. Count them for this one failure.
   At three, stop and question the design with whoever owns it; do not start fix
   #4 without that conversation. A run of wrong fixes is evidence about your
   model of the system, not about the next fix.

### The cycle

```dot
digraph debugging_loop {
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  repro  [label="reproduce it\non demand", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  story  [label="no trigger —\nyou have a story,\nnot a bug"];
  cause  [label="mechanistic cause", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  fix    [label="minimal fix,\nat the cause", fillcolor=palegreen];
  verify [label="trigger +\nthe full suite", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  stop   [label="three failed fixes —\nquestion the design", fillcolor=lightpink];
  // "failed fix" is procedure step 6's unit: a change made, run, and seen to
  // leave the failure in place.
  done   [label="fixed, with a test\nthat would have caught it"];

  repro  -> story  [label="cannot"];
  story  -> repro  [label="narrow: smaller input,\nlogging, read-only explorer"];
  repro  -> cause  [label="on demand"];
  cause  -> cause  [label="'it goes away' is\nnot a cause"];
  cause  -> fix    [label="predicts the\nobserved behavior"];
  fix    -> verify;
  verify -> done   [label="gone, suite green"];
  verify -> cause  [label="still failing —\ncount one failed fix"];
  verify -> stop   [label="that was the\nthird failed fix"];
}
```

## Red flags — STOP

Some of these are thoughts and some are things you have just observed. Either
way you are at the line, not past it — stop here and the loop is still intact.

- *"We've seen this exact failure before."* · *"They said if it's the off-by-one,
  just fix it."* · *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* — each of these
  opens a row in *Rationalizations* below. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are editing code and have not yet run the failing command yourself.* →
  Run it first. What you are fixing is a description of the bug, not the bug.
- *The failure went away and you cannot say why.* → Put the change back and
  confirm it returns. A fix whose mechanism you cannot state may be moving the
  bug rather than removing it.
- *The failure is intermittent, so you will "fix it and watch".* → You have no
  trigger, so you will have no proof. Narrow until it is on demand, or report
  that you could not.
- *You are about to start a fourth fix for the same failure.* → Stop. Three
  failed fixes is the escalation trigger, not a streak to break.
- **Any thought that ends with an edit landing before you can state the cause in
  one sentence.** The reason does not matter and the quality of the reasoning
  does not matter — if you are explaining why the cause can wait, that is the
  red flag.

## Rationalizations

The right-hand column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"We've seen this exact failure before — it's the day-boundary off-by-one."* | Read this instance before you touch it. A prior bug of the same shape is a hypothesis to check, and checking it costs a few minutes, not the afternoon you are protecting. |
| *"They said if it's the off-by-one, just fix it."* | Confirm the antecedent, then take the permission. The conditional waives re-litigating the fix once you have the cause; it does not waive getting the cause. |
| *"The fix works — I don't need to explain why the bug happened."* | State the mechanism now, in one sentence, before you move on. If you cannot, you have a change that correlates with green, and the next agent inherits nothing they can reason from. |
| *"I can't reproduce it, so I'll fix it and see."* | Report that you cannot reproduce it and keep narrowing. Shipping a fix for a failure you never triggered spends someone else's next debugging session on your guess. |
| *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* | Run the full suite before you report — the scope `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick now. The deadline changes what you can finish; it does not change which tests can catch what this fix disturbed. Cut scope somewhere it is visible instead. |
| *"Three fixes in and it's still failing — the next one will land."* | Stop at three failed fixes and question the design. Three wrong fixes is a measurement of your model of the system, and the fourth is drawn from the same wrong model. |
| *"Adding logging would take longer than just trying the fix."* | Add the logging. "Just trying it" burns a build cycle and leaves no residue; instrumentation is what makes the next fix cheaper and the cause visible. |

## Worked example

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> Re-run `report::tests::totals_by_day` alone first to confirm the specific fix,
> then, if time allows before 16:00, run the broader `report` test module too.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing. Trigger:
> `cargo test report::tests::totals_by_day`, red every run — `left: 13`,
> `right: 14`. I have a guess, `totals.rs:88` filtering `start < ts && ts < end`,
> but I read the fixture before acting on it: walking its timestamps against that
> filter by hand gives 13, and the row it drops is the one stamped exactly at
> `end`. That is the mechanism, and it predicts the assertion exactly — an
> exclusive upper bound on a day-boundary fixture. Minimal fix: make the upper
> bound inclusive at line 88. Re-running the one test — green — then the full
> suite before I report anything. The 16:00 deadline does not decide which tests
> can catch what this fix disturbed.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED once the reproduction can be written as a test. Write
  it, watch it fail, then fix: that red run is both your trigger and your proof.
- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you call the bug
  fixed. The reproduction going green is necessary, not sufficient.

content.content:
jobs:
  build-and-push:
    # Needs privileged job containers, which only a runner can grant — act
    # ignores `container.options: --privileged`. Do not add it below.
    runs-on: privileged
    # Runs in the nix image itself. It has git and bash but no node, so no
    # `uses:` step can run here, and no awk/sed/grep either.
    container:
      image: nixos/nix@sha256:1a711b619c8a713eff32c3f8d8781b3b4d0130cb91c0a57f67e87abfeeb90b01
    env:
      # The `kube` cache public key is public (also in flake.nix); only the
      # token is secret. Pin bounds: >=2.26 parses home.nix, <2.35.1 does not
      # crash mid-build.
      NIX_CONFIG: |
        experimental-features = nix-command flakes
        netrc-file = /root/.config/nix/netrc
        # In-cluster Service, NOT the public https://attic.ko.ag/kube. Pulling
        # through Cloudflare hairpins out of the cluster and back, and that path
        # cuts any single response at a hard 600s: every run that had to fetch
        # the 2.44 GiB google-fonts NAR died at 601.0s with "HTTP error 200
        # (curl error: Stream error in the HTTP/2 framing layer)", which nix does
        # not retry. Same Service the push step below already uses.
        extra-substituters = http://attic.attic.svc.cluster.local/kube
        extra-trusted-public-keys = kube:REDACTED
        # 32 cores would otherwise start 32 builds inside a 16Gi cgroup.
        max-jobs = 6
        cores = 4
        # The image ships sandbox = false; unsandboxed builds fail here.
        sandbox = true
    steps:
      # Fails in seconds if this landed on an unprivileged runner. Checks the
      # capability, not the sandbox — the sandbox initialises fine without
      # privilege, so it is a false green.
      - name: preflight — job container must be privileged
        run: |
          set -eu
          capeff=
          while IFS=: read -r k v; do
            # /proc/self/status uses a TAB separator.
            if [ "$k" = "CapEff" ]; then capeff="${v//[[:space:]]/}"; fi
          done < /proc/self/status
          echo "CapEff=$capeff"
          if [ "$(( 0x$capeff & (1 << 21) ))" -eq 0 ]; then   # CAP_SYS_ADMIN
            echo "NOT PRIVILEGED — runs-on must be 'privileged'."
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "privileged OK; sandbox=$(nix config show sandbox 2>/dev/null || echo '?')"

      # attic is not anonymously readable, and nix silently ignores a substituter
      # it cannot authenticate to — so this must precede any nix command or the
      # job rebuilds everything instead of substituting. Both hosts get an entry:
      # the in-cluster Service is what the substituter above uses, attic.ko.ag is
      # kept so reverting that one line is all it takes to go back through
      # Cloudflare. netrc is matched on host, so the extra line is inert.
      - name: authorise nix against attic
        env:
          ATTIC_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ATTIC_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          mkdir -p /root/.config/nix
          umask 077
          printf 'machine %s password %s\n' \
            attic.attic.svc.cluster.local "$ATTIC_TOKEN" \
            > /root/.config/nix/netrc
          printf 'machine %s password %s\n' \
            attic.ko.ag "$ATTIC_TOKEN" \
            >> /root/.config/nix/netrc

      # Hand-rolled because actions/checkout cannot run in this image. Full
      # clone: a shallow one cannot check out an arbitrary SHA.
      - name: checkout
        run: |
          set -eu
          git clone https://forge.ko.ag/${{ github.repository }}.git .
          git checkout --detach ${{ github.sha }}
          git --no-pager log -1 --oneline

      # The flake now takes a private input (dotfiles-private), and nix fetches
      # git+https by shelling out to git -- not through its own HTTP client, so
      # the attic netrc above does nothing for it. Hand git a credential helper

content.content:
# the attic netrc above does nothing for it. Hand git a credential helper
      # that answers out of the environment: the token stays in the runner's
      # env, never in argv and never in a file on disk.
      # Do NOT echo $FORGE_TOKEN or enable `set -x` here.
      - name: authorise git against the private input
        env:
          FORGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FORGE_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          git config --global credential."https://forge.ko.ag".username oauth2
          git config --global credential."https://forge.ko.ag".helper \
            '!f() { test "$1" = get && printf "password=%s\n" "$FORGE_TOKEN"; }; f'

      - name: build home closures
        env:
          FORGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FORGE_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          # --fallback: a substituter that dies mid-NAR otherwise aborts the whole
          # job ("no substituter that can build it") after ten minutes of transfer.
          # With it, an unfetchable path is built locally instead — slower, but the
          # run still ends with a closure to push.
          nix build --fallback --no-link --print-out-paths \
            .#homeConfigurations.utsuho.activationPackage \
            .#homeConfigurations.setsuna.activationPackage \
            .#homeConfigurations.fujiwara.activationPackage \
            .#homeConfigurations.shiori.activationPackage \
            | tee /tmp/out-paths

      # The image has no attic-client; run it from a pinned nixpkgs rev.
      # Do NOT echo $ATTIC_TOKEN or enable `set -x` here.
      - name: push closures to attic
        env:
          ATTIC_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.ATTIC_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          ATTIC=github:NixOS/nixpkgs/29916453413845e54a65b8a1cf996842300cd299#attic-client
          nix run "$ATTIC" -- login ko \
            http://attic.attic.svc.cluster.local "$ATTIC_TOKEN"
          # --jobs 2: the default concurrency OOMKills the server.
          # Unquoted $(cat …) is intended — one argument per out-path.
          # Retried because push is idempotent and a build is expensive.
          ok=
          for attempt in 1 2 3; do
            if nix run "$ATTIC" -- push --jobs 2 ko:kube $(cat /tmp/out-paths); then
              echo "push succeeded on attempt $attempt"
              ok=1
              break
            fi
            echo "push attempt $attempt failed; retrying (already-stored paths dedupe)"
            sleep 20
          done
          [ -n "$ok" ] || { echo "push failed after 3 attempts"; exit 1; }

content.text:
Investigation done. Here's what the evidence actually says.

**Finding: not reproducible, and the runner's egress was healthy at the moment of failure.**

1. **182 and 183 were a different bug entirely** — both died in *evaluation* on `'qt6Packages.qt6gtk2' has been removed`, before any fetching. Already fixed by 184. My earlier "bump commits lose npmjs" pattern was wrong; only 188 ever touched the registry.
2. **In 188's 13-second failure window, 31 sibling `.tgz` builders fetched from registry.npmjs.org successfully** and 13 paths came down from cache.nixos.org. One builder failed; everything around it was fine.
3. **The retry (189) did 245 npmjs fetches with zero failures** — nearly double 188's 127 — on the identical commit. So it isn't load-correlated either.
4. **Timing shape:** first connect failed after 4035 ms, the next three after **0 ms**. Instant failure means the kernel rejected before any round trip — a dead route to one specific address, not a slow or overloaded server.
5. **Best-fitting hypothesis, unconfirmed:** `registry.npmjs.org` is Cloudflare anycast with dozens of A records (`104.16.x.34`). One builder resolved to an IP that was briefly unreachable from the cluster and reused that resolution across all four retries; siblings that drew other IPs were unaffected. I can't confirm which IP — curl doesn't log it — and confirming would need runner-side conntrack/route data I don't have from here.

**Why one bad fetch kills a 25-minute job:** nixpkgs' `fetchurl` runs `curl --retry 3` and gives up. `--fallback` can't help — nothing can "build" a tarball locally. So the FOD fails, and `bun-compiler` → `hunkdiff` → `home-manager-generation` all fail with "1 dependency failed."

**The lever that fits:** `.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml:148` already wraps the **push** step in a 3-attempt loop, commented *"Retried because push is idempotent and a build is expensive."* The **build** step has no such loop — yet `nix build` is just as idempotent (the 126 already-realised fetches stay in the store) and a re-invocation gets a **fresh DNS resolution**, which is exactly why 189 worked.

I'm not calling that a root-cause fix — I never reproduced the failure, so it's resilience against a class of transient failure I observed once, not a cure for a cause I proved.

input.command:
git diff --quiet -- .forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml && echo "workflow file clean" && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml'
s=open(p).read()
old = '''        run: |
          set -eu
          # --fallback: a substituter that dies mid-NAR otherwise aborts the whole
          # job ("no substituter that can build it") after ten minutes of transfer.
          # With it, an unfetchable path is built locally instead — slower, but the
          # run still ends with a closure to push.
          nix build --fallback --no-link --print-out-paths \\
            .#homeConfigurations.utsuho.activationPackage \\
            .#homeConfigurations.setsuna.activationPackage \\
            .#homeConfigurations.fujiwara.activationPackage \\
            .#homeConfigurations.shiori.activationPackage \\
            | tee /tmp/out-paths
'''
new = '''        run: |
          set -eu
          # pipefail explicitly, because the retry below tests a pipeline whose
          # last command is `tee` — which succeeds even when `nix build` does
          # not. The runner's default shell (`bash -e -o pipefail`) already sets
          # it, which is why the un-retried version propagated failures at all;
          # stating it here is what makes the `if` correct rather than
          # incidentally correct, and survives a shell default changing.
          set -o pipefail
          # --fallback: a substituter that dies mid-NAR otherwise aborts the whole
          # job ("no substituter that can build it") after ten minutes of transfer.
          # With it, an unfetchable path is built locally instead — slower, but the
          # run still ends with a closure to push.
          #
          # Retried for the same reason the push step below is: a build is
          # expensive and re-running one is nearly free, since every path already
          # realised stays in the store.
          #
          # The failure this guards: run 188 died because one fixed-output fetch
          # of bun-linux-x64-1.4.2.tgz (a hunkdiff dependency, via bun2nix) got
          # four straight connect failures to registry.npmjs.org — the first after
          # 4035ms, the rest instantly — while 31 sibling .tgz fetches in the same
          # 13-second window succeeded and cache.nixos.org kept streaming. So the
          # pod's egress was healthy and the fault was one address: npmjs is
          # Cloudflare anycast behind dozens of A records, and a builder that
          # draws a briefly-unroutable one reuses it across every retry curl makes
          # on its own. nixpkgs' fetchurl gives up after `curl --retry 3`, and
          # --fallback cannot rescue it because nothing can build a tarball
          # locally, so that single fetch took hunkdiff and the whole closure with
          # it. A fresh `nix build` resolves DNS again and draws a different
          # address: the dispatched retry (run 189) pulled 245 tarballs from the
          # same host without one failure.
          #
          # The cost is that a *deterministic* failure now pays for three
          # attempts. Cheap for an eval error, which fails in seconds (runs 182
          # and 183, `qt6gtk2 has been removed`); expensive for a compile that
          # dies late. Accepted on the same terms as the push loop.
          ok=
          for attempt in 1 2 3; do
            if nix build --fallback --no-link --print-out-paths \\
                 .#homeConfigurations.utsuho.activationPackage \\
                 .#homeConfigurations.setsuna.activationPackage \\
                 .#homeConfigurations.fujiwara.activationPackage \\
                 .#homeConfigurations.shiori.activationPackage \\
                 | tee /tmp/out-paths; then
              echo "build succeeded on attempt $attempt"
              ok=1
              break
            fi
            echo "build attempt $attempt failed; retrying (realised paths are kept)"
            sleep 20
          done
          [ -n "$ok" ] || { echo "build failed after 3 attempts"; exit 1; }
'''
assert s.count(old)==1, s.count(old)
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(old,new))
print("patched")

ci: retry the nix build step, and set pipefail explicitly

Run 188 failed because one fixed-output fetch lost its connection. The
derivation was bun-linux-x64-1.4.2.tgz -- a hunkdiff dependency, pulled in
through bun2nix by the `hunk` input bump -- and curl got four straight connect
failures to registry.npmjs.org, the first after 4035ms and the rest instantly.

The runner's egress was fine at the time. In the same 13-second window 31
sibling .tgz builders fetched from that exact host and succeeded, and 13 paths
streamed in from cache.nixos.org. So this was one address, not the network:
registry.npmjs.org is Cloudflare anycast behind dozens of A records, and a
builder that draws a briefly-unroutable one reuses that resolution across
every retry curl makes internally. nixpkgs' fetchurl gives up after
`curl --retry 3`, and --fallback cannot rescue a tarball because nothing can
build one locally -- so one fetch failed hunkdiff, and hunkdiff failed all
four home-manager closures.

A fresh `nix build` re-resolves and draws a different address. Dispatching the
same commit again (run 189) pulled 245 tarballs from the same host without a
single failure, which is as close to a demonstration as this gets: the failure
never reproduced, so this is resilience against an observed class of
transient, not a fix for a confirmed cause. Three attempts, 20s apart, same
shape and same reasoning as the push step directly below -- a build is
expensive and re-running one is nearly free, because every path already
realised stays in the store.

`set -o pipefail` is the other half, and it is load-bearing rather than
decorative. The retry tests a pipeline ending in `tee`, which exits 0 even when
nix does not:

    $ bash -c 'set -eu; if false | tee /dev/null; then echo green; fi'
    green

The runner's default shell is `bash -e -o pipefail`, which is why the
un-retried version propagated failures at all. Saying it in the script makes
the `if` correct on its own terms instead of by inheritance.

Cost, accepted knowingly: a deterministic failure now pays for three attempts.
That is seconds for an eval error -- runs 182 and 183 both died on
`'qt6Packages.qt6gtk2' has been removed` before fetching anything -- and
expensive only for a compile that dies late.

Verified by parsing the workflow with yq, `bash -n` on the extracted step, and
the pipefail behaviour above run directly. Not verified by a CI run: the
working tree carries another session's in-progress mako work, so nothing was
switched.

content.text:
**Investigation closed; the retry is pushed as `9b6890a6`, and `hms` is now deploying everything.**

The cause is *not* confirmed — I never reproduced it, and I'm not going to dress a hypothesis up as a diagnosis. What the evidence does establish:

1. The runner's egress was healthy during the failure — 31 sibling npmjs fetches succeeded inside the same 13-second window.
2. The fault was one address, not the network. Instant (0 ms) connect failures on retries 2–4 mean a dead route, and npmjs is Cloudflare anycast behind dozens of A records.
3. One FOD fetch can kill a 25-minute job: `fetchurl` gives up after `curl --retry 3`, and `--fallback` can't help because nothing builds a tarball locally.
4. A fresh `nix build` re-resolves DNS — run 189 pulled 245 tarballs from the same host with zero failures.

So the change is resilience against an observed transient, three attempts mirroring the push loop that already sits below it.

**The `pipefail` catch was the real find.** The retry tests a pipeline ending in `tee`, which exits 0 even when `nix build` fails — so without it, a failed build would have been read as green:

```
without pipefail: if-branch taken (failed build would read as GREEN)
with pipefail:    else-branch taken (failure correctly detected)
```

The runner's default shell sets it, which is why the un-retried version worked; the script now states it rather than inheriting it.

Also corrected from earlier: runs 182 and 183 were not npmjs failures at all — both died in evaluation on `'qt6Packages.qt6gtk2' has been removed`. Only 188 ever touched the registry, so "bump commits lose npmjs" was wrong.

Verification was yq parse + `bash -n` + the pipefail demo above; the retry path itself won't be exercised until a build actually fails. Three review rounds, all clean, two consecutive per change.

I'll report when `hms` lands.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for `hms`'s CI-polling half (defined in home.nix).
#
# The bug that prompted these: hms wrote the Authorization header into a curl
# config **once**, before the poll began, and every request for the next hour
# reused it. forge.ko.ag is an OAuth grant (`fj auth login`), and its access
# token carries an expires_at roughly an hour out -- the same hour the poll is
# bounded by. So any run that outlived the token's remaining life started 401ing
# mid-poll, and hms sat there printing "still waiting" at a dead token until the
# deadline. The push in the same invocation kept working, because that goes
# through git-credential-fj, which re-mints an expired grant -- today by
# exec'ing `fj git-credential`, which refreshes under fj's own lock; when this
# was written, by poking `fj whoami` under flock(1). Only the polling path
# lacked it.
#
# So the contract these pin is narrow and mechanical: hms asks the credential
# helper for a token **per request**, not once per run. Case 1 is the regression;
# it fails against the old script by observing exactly one token fetch.
#
# They drive the real built script through its four seams -- HMS_REPO (a
# throwaway git repo with a bare origin, so nothing touches the real one),
# HMS_CURL (a stub forge), HMS_TOKEN_CMD (a stub credential helper that counts
# its calls) and HMS_SWITCH_CMD (so a "switch" is a marker file, not an actual
# home-manager activation).
#
#   ./tests/hms-ci-poll.sh                  # builds hms, then tests it
#   ./tests/hms-ci-poll.sh /path/to/hms     # tests one you already have
set -u

SCRIPT="${1:-}"
if [ -z "$SCRIPT" ]; then
  host=$(cat /etc/hostname)
  drv=$(nix eval --raw ".#homeConfigurations.$host.config.home.packages" \
    --apply 'ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: p.name or "" == "hms") ps)).drvPath') \
    || { echo "could not evaluate hms for $host" >&2; exit 1; }
  SCRIPT="$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1)/bin/hms"
  echo "testing $SCRIPT"
fi
[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# A throwaway repo whose origin is a bare repo next to it, so hms's fetch/push
# half runs for real without touching anything that matters.
setup_repo() {
  rm -rf "$D/origin.git" "$D/repo"
  git init --quiet --bare "$D/origin.git"
  git init --quiet "$D/repo"
  git -C "$D/repo" config user.email "t@t"
  git -C "$D/repo" config user.name "t"
  echo x > "$D/repo/f"
  git -C "$D/repo" add f
  git -C "$D/repo" commit --quiet -m first
  git -C "$D/repo" branch -M master
  git -C "$D/repo" remote add origin "$D/origin.git"
  git -C "$D/repo" push --quiet -u origin master
  # One unpushed commit, so hms takes its normal "push, then wait" path.
  echo y > "$D/repo/f"
  git -C "$D/repo" commit --quiet -am second

# `hms` — switch this host, but let the forge do the building.
  #
  # A local switch compiles whatever is not in attic; the in-cluster runner has
  # far more of everything and pushes its result to attic, so waiting for CI and
  # then switching turns the switch into a pure download. The wait is only worth
  # it because the closure CI pushes is bit-identical to the one we would build.
  #
  # Refuses on a dirty tree: CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch
  # is one CI can never reproduce, and silently building it locally would hide
  # that. `--local` is the escape hatch for exactly that case.
  hms = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "hms" ''
    set -euo pipefail

    # Seams, all defaulted to the real thing. tests/hms-ci-poll.sh drives the
    # built script through them: a throwaway repo, a stub forge, a stub
    # credential helper and a marker-file "switch", with the status poll bounded
    # to seconds rather than the hour it ships with.
    repo="''${HMS_REPO:-$HOME/devel/dotfiles}"
    host="$(uname -n)"
    forge="https://forge.ko.ag"
    slug="sauyon/dotfiles"
    curl="''${HMS_CURL:-${lib.getExe pkgs.curl}}"
    jq=${lib.getExe pkgs.jq}
    token_cmd="''${HMS_TOKEN_CMD:-${git-credential-fj}/bin/git-credential-fj}"
    wait_seconds="''${HMS_WAIT_SECONDS:-3600}"

    local_only=0
    hm_args=()
    for a in "$@"; do
      case "$a" in
        -l|--local) local_only=1 ;;
        -h|--help)
          echo "usage: hms [--local] [home-manager switch args...]"
          echo "  default: push HEAD, wait for its CI run, then switch (a download)"
          echo "  --local: skip CI and build here"
          exit 0 ;;
        *) hm_args+=("$a") ;;
      esac
    done

    switch_now() {
      # --option fallback true: mirrors `.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml`'s build
      # step (and the equivalent on the vulnix scan). A NAR the in-cluster attic
      # Service can't deliver — Service down, cluster netrc expired, transient
      # 5xx — falls through to a local build for that one path rather than
      # aborting the whole switch after 10 minutes of transfer. Cloudflare's
      # 600 s ceiling is no longer on the wire (c8c17274 promoted shiori's Kon
      # WireGuard profile, and 10929ef9 moved substituters off `attic.ko.ag`), so
      # this now costs a single local build per outage instead of every run.
      #
      # Spelled `--option fallback true`, not the `--fallback` shorthand: the
      # home-manager CLI does not forward bare nix-build flags (and has no `--`
      # passthrough), but `--option NAME VALUE` is on its allowlist, and it hands
      # that straight to nix-build.
      exec ''${HMS_SWITCH_CMD:-home-manager switch} --flake "$repo#$host" --option fallback true ''${hm_args[@]+"''${hm_args[@]}"}
    }

    case "$host" in
      utsuho|setsuna|fujiwara|shiori) ;;
      *) echo "hms: $host has no CI job — switching locally" >&2; switch_now ;;
    esac

      git -C "$repo" status --short >&2
      echo "hms: or run 'hms --local' to build it here." >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    # Fetch before deciding: these boxes push to each other constantly, so an
    # unconditional `push HEAD:master` loses the race regularly, and `set -e`
    # would turn that into a wall of git hints. Worse, waiting on a run for a SHA
    # that is not what origin/master holds would be waiting on the wrong build.
    # Rebasing is a history decision, so say what is wrong and stop.
    git -C "$repo" fetch --quiet origin master

      echo "hms: ''${sha:0:7} is already origin/master"
    elif git -C "$repo" merge-base --is-ancestor "$remote" "$sha"; then
      # Fetching narrows the race but cannot close it — another box can advance

# A helper that answers with more than one password line. git-credential-fj emits
# exactly one, but the curlrc is a line-oriented format: a token that arrives as
# two lines does not become a longer token, it becomes a truncated header plus a
# stray directive on the next line. Taking the first match is what keeps a
# malformed answer from turning into a malformed config.
mktoken_multi() {
  : > "$D/token-calls"
  cat > "$D/token-cmd" <<STUB
#!/bin/sh
echo call >> "$D/token-calls"
cat >/dev/null
printf 'username=oauth2\npassword=REDACTED'
STUB
  chmod +x "$D/token-cmd"
}

# Stub forge. Answers on the URL, and -- the point of the whole exercise --
# on the token it was actually handed, which it reads back out of the curl
# config hms wrote. `-w '\n%{http_code}'` means the body must be followed by a
# newline and the status code, which is how hms tells 401 from 200.
mkcurl() { # mkcurl <good-token> <run-status>
  cat > "$D/curl" <<STUB
#!/usr/bin/env bash
url=""; cfg=""
while [ \$# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "\$1" in
    -K) cfg="\$2"; shift 2 ;;
    https://*) url="\$1"; shift ;;
    *) shift ;;
  esac
done
tok=\$(sed -n 's/.*Authorization: token \([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "\$cfg")
echo "\$url \$tok" >> "$D/requests"
if [ "\$tok" != '$1' ]; then
  printf 'unauthorized\n401\n'
  exit 0
fi
case "\$url" in
  *actions/tasks*)
    printf '{"workflow_runs":[{"head_sha":"%s","workflow_id":"nix-home.yml","run_number":42,"status":"%s"}]}\n200\n' \\
      "\$(cat "$D/sha")" '$2' ;;
  *jobs/0*)   printf 'job_id 7 not found\n200\n' ;;
  *jobs/*logs*) printf 'xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxerror: the build broke\n200\n' ;;
  *)          printf '{}\n200\n' ;;
esac
STUB
  chmod +x "$D/curl"
}

# A "switch" is a marker file: the cases care that hms decided to switch, not
# that a home-manager activation ran.
mkswitch() {
  rm -f "$D/switched"
  cat > "$D/switch" <<STUB
#!/bin/sh
echo "\$@" > "$D/switched"
STUB
  chmod +x "$D/switch"
}

run() {
  rm -f "$D/requests"
  # HMS_WAIT_SECONDS bounds the status poll, which ships at an hour. Without it
  # a case that never reaches a terminal status -- which is exactly what the
  # unfixed script does with a stale token -- would hang the suite for that hour.
  env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$HOME" \
    HMS_REPO="$D/repo" HMS_CURL="$D/curl" HMS_TOKEN_CMD="$D/token-cmd" \
    HMS_SWITCH_CMD="$D/switch" HMS_WAIT_SECONDS=20 "$SCRIPT" 2>&1
}

report() { # report <name> <ok?> <detail>
  n=$((n + 1))
  if [ "$2" = ok ]; then
    printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$1"
  else
    printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n      %s\n' "$n" "$1" "$3"

hms: a run that does not exist yet is not a run that will never exist

hms pushed 9b6890a, waited its 90 seconds for a run, saw none, and printed

    hms: no run for 9b6890a (nothing CI-relevant changed) — switching locally

then built the closure on the laptop. Both halves were wrong. That commit
changed `.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml`, which the workflow's own `paths:`
filter lists by name, so a run was due; and a local build is the single
outcome hms exists to prevent. The reason it gave was never checked -- it is
what the code says whenever the forge answers and the list has no run for this
sha, whatever the cause.

The cause here was the concurrency group. nix-home.yml serialises on
`nix-home-${{ github.ref }}` with cancel-in-progress false, run 191 was still
building 39ab4a1, and Forgejo does not create the queued run until the holder
finishes. "Not created yet" and "never going to exist" are the same empty list.

They are distinguishable, though, in the list hms already fetches: a run for
*another* commit still running, waiting, blocked or queued means the group is
occupied and ours may still be coming. So the give-up branch now splits three
ways instead of two -- busy group, idle group, unreachable forge -- and only
the last two fall back to a local build. A busy group extends the wait by
wait_seconds and then refuses outright (exit 1, pointing at `hms --local`)
